slides.title: Spoken Tutorial on Understanding APIs
slides.narration: Welcome to this Spoken Tutorial on **Understanding APIs**.

slides.title: Learning Objectives
slides.narration:
In this tutorial, you will learn to,
• Define what an **API** is.
• Explain **prompts** and **API keys**.
• Identify how applications interact with **APIs**.

slides.title: System Requirements
slides.narration: Here I am using a browser on a computer or mobile.

slides.title: Prerequisites
slides.narration: To follow this tutorial, you should have watched **Episode 1: Python basics for API**.

slides.title: What is an API? & The Connector Analogy
slides.narration:
Have you ever wondered how different apps talk to each other?
They use something called an **API**.
**API** stands for **Application Programming Interface**.
It is a set of rules that lets software programs communicate.
Think of a restaurant.
You, the customer, order from the waiter.
The waiter takes your order to the kitchen.
The kitchen prepares food and gives it back to the waiter.
The waiter then brings your food to you.
Here, the waiter is the **API**.
It connects you to the kitchen without you knowing details.
Similarly, an **API** connects different software parts.
slides.image_prompt: Restaurant analogy: waiter connecting customer and kitchen

slides.title: Prompts as Inputs and API Keys
slides.narration:
With that understanding, let's look at how we use **APIs**.
When you use an **AI** tool, you give it a **prompt**.
A **prompt** is simply the input data you send to the **API**.
For example, asking **ChatGPT** a question is a **prompt**.
But how does the **API** know who you are?
This is where **API keys** come in.
An **API key** is a unique code.
It acts like a digital ID card or a password.
You send your **API key** with your **prompt**.
This key authenticates your request.
It ensures only authorized users can access the **API**.
slides.image_prompt: Person at laptop, illustration of prompt going into API and API key unlocking access

slides.title: Vague Example: Sending a Request
slides.narration:
Now, let's see a simple example of sending a request.
Imagine an application wants to use an **AI** model.
It might try to send a **prompt** directly like this.
See how the request is very basic.
There is no clear structure for the data.
Also, there is no **API key** included.
This method is unoptimized and unsecured.
It is like shouting your order in a restaurant.
The kitchen might not understand you.
Or, it might not know who placed the order.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Imagine an application wants to use an AI model...'

slides.title: Improved Example: Sending a Request
slides.narration:
Now, let's look at an improved way to send a request.
Here, the application sends a structured request.
Notice the data is organized, perhaps in JSON format.
It clearly states the **prompt** and other parameters.
Most importantly, an **API key** is included for authentication.
This is like giving a clear, written order to the waiter.
You also show your membership card for access.
The **API** can now process this request efficiently.
It knows who you are and what you want.
slides.image_prompt: Screen close-up: user typing 'Here, the application sends a structured request...'

slides.title: Comparing Request Methods
slides.narration:
Let us compare these two request methods.
On one side, we have the vague, unstructured request.
On the other, the improved, structured request.
See the difference in clarity and security?
The improved method uses a clear data format.
It also includes the essential **API key**.
This ensures your request is understood and authorized.
It also protects your access to the **API**.
Using structured requests and **API keys** is vital.
It makes your application's interaction with **APIs** reliable.
slides.image_prompt: Side-by-side: vague prompt output vs improved prompt output

slides.title: Summary
slides.narration:
Let us summarize what we learned.
We defined what an **API** is, like a digital waiter.
We saw how **prompts** are inputs to **APIs**.
We understood that **API keys** control access.
Finally, we compared different ways to send requests.

slides.title: Assignment
slides.narration:
Now as an assignment,
Think about an app you use daily.
How might it use an **API** to function?
Describe the **prompts** and potential data flow.
Compare your thoughts with a friend.
